title: Ai Weiwei helped design Beijing's Olympic stadium. But he regrets how it's being used today
text:
arts
Ai Weiwei helped design Beijing's Olympic stadium. But he regrets how it's being used today
Updated 4th February 2022
Credit: Chris J. Ratcliffe/Bloomberg/Getty Images
Ai Weiwei helped design Beijing's Olympic stadium. But he regrets how it's being used today
Christiane Amanpour's interview with Ai Weiwei airs Friday 1pm ET. See more here.
As the Beijing Winter Olympics gets underway, artist Ai Weiwei is once again criticizing China's ruling Communist Party -- and the International Olympic Committee (IOC), which he said is "ignoring" the safety of the country's athletes by prioritizing business and "standing next to the authoritarians."
The world-renowned Chinese dissident and rights activist made the comments to CNN's Christiane Amanpour in an interview from Portugal, where he has been living in self-exile since 2021. Fearing for his safety were he to return to China, where he was once detained for 81 days for "inciting the subversion of state power," Ai has resided around Europe for almost seven years.
Years prior to his departure from his home country, Ai famously consulted on the design of the venue hosting Friday night's opening ceremony: The Beijing National Stadium, or "Bird's Nest."
The open-roofed structure, wrapped in interwoven streel structs, functioned as one of the main venues for the Summer Olympics in 2008. A collaboration with Swiss architecture firm Herzog & de Meuron, the stadium took five years to build and was designed to represent a new, modern China.
But the artist distanced himself from the project and criticized China's hosting of the Olympics ahead of the opening ceremony, believing it to be a propaganda tool at odds with what he felt were the oppressive realities of life in the country.
"Unfortunately, as an architect, you cannot control how the building is being used," Ai told Amanpour in the interview, which airs Friday. "For me it's a big disappointment, not only in how it's being used but also in the directions China (has taken) in past decades."
In his recently published book "1000 Years of Joys and Sorrows," Ai wrote about the stadium's design, which was inspired by the art of Chinese ceramics. It "aimed to convey the message that freedom was possible," he wrote, and "encapsulated something essential about democracy, transparency and equity."
"We have to defend everybody who has been mistreated, and only by doing that, can we build a better future."
When asked if he really believed, back then, that China would become democratic, free and transparent, Ai responded, "Well, by that time, of course I believed so. But at this moment, I doubt (it)," adding that that the country has, in many ways, gone "backwards."
In the lead up to this year's Winter games, which Ai has also been openly critical of, China has been subjected to increased international scrutiny, from its alleged human rights abuses in Xinjiang to its stringent Covid-19 policies to the global concern for the well-being of Chinese tennis player and three-time Olympian, Peng Shuai. Peng disappeared from public view for over two weeks after she accused a former top Communist Party official of sexual assault.
Beijing denies allegations of human rights abuses and has dismissed fears for Peng's safety as "malicious speculation." The IOC, meanwhile, did not respond directly to Ai's accusations, but said in a statement to CNN that it "recognizes and upholds human rights," which are "enshrined" in both the Olympic Charter and the organization's code of ethics. "Given the diverse participation in the Olympic Games," read the statement, "the IOC must remain neutral on global political issues."
But Ai argued that the IOC has "never" been neutral. "They're always standing next to the authoritarians or business," he told Amanpour. "Since the 2008 Olympics, they have been working with the government's propaganda, and this time they are (doing so) even more. They are ignoring the top (Chinese) athletes' safety and well-being."
While the dissident artist has not called for athletes to boycott the games, he appealed to their "sense of justice and fairness," adding: "The Games is about fairness, the competition is about fairness. And so, athletes representing human spirit (should) of course defend those very important issues, such as human rights and freedom of speech.
A 'citizen of nowhere'
Ai said he wrote "1000 Years of Joys and Sorrows," his first memoir, to show young people what he called the "absurd" reality of living in China.
"I have to write (for) my son's generation to understand what really happened to his father and his grandfather," he told Amanpour. Ai's father, a poet who was also accused of subverting state power, spent time in jail and was sent to a labor camp in Xinjiang when Ai was a child. Ai later joined him in the far northwestern region where, today, China has been accused of genocide by the United States against Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities.
Ai said he ultimately left China in 2015 because he lacked a "sense of safety" as an artist. His conceptual works, many of which were considered controversial in China, often contend with the country's past and present using found objects. He has created sculptures from the remains of demolished Ming and Qing dynasty houses, as well as from steel rods salvaged from schools that collapsed during the deadly 2008 Sichuan earthquake. One of his most famous works, a photo triptych from 1995, shows him smashing a Han dynasty urn.
"China is totally under the control of one party, and the party can do anything," he said of his reasons for living in self-exile. "It can make you disappear. It can make you (go on) trial without lawyers. And also, they can put you (for) a long time behind bars. Nobody can (argue with authorities) -- that's the reality. So, if I want to have a sense of safety, a normal life, I have to escape."
Ai has been critical of other countries too, particularly when it comes to the West's treatment of refugees.
"I'm a citizen of the world, if I can call it that. Actually, I'm a citizen of nowhere," he told Amanpour. "So, wherever I see injustice, I always think that's connected. Whatever happens in Afghanistan, in Syria, is connected to China (and) also connected to the United States. We have to understand humanity as one, human rights as one. We have to defend everybody who has been mistreated, and only by doing that, can we build a better future."

title: Council Post: 5 Digital Marketing Tactics To Drive Profits In 2022
text:
Bernard May is the CEO of National Positions, a 5-time Inc. 500 company, award-winning marketing agency and Google Premier Partner.
Whether you’re a startup or an established brand, marketing never stops evolving. There’s no time to rest as we continue full steam ahead into another new year.
Marketing in 2022 will require listening intently to what customers want and being responsive to their needs as competition grows ever-more fierce. Here are five digital marketing strategies to help you make the most of 2022.
1. Treat your first-party data like gold.
Advertisers and marketers are on their toes as growing consumer privacy concerns force traditional third-party data collection into the dustbin of history. Safari and Firefox have already banned website cookies. Google will scrap them on Chrome (which represents nearly 70% of market share) in 2023.
Brands need to adopt new strategies for connecting with customers. That means capitalizing on the “gold” sitting right under their noses. I’m talking about first-party data. Customer data from sources like completed on-site purchases, surveys, customer feedback and your CRM is valuable for two big reasons. First, because you own it. Second, it gives you the blueprint for your ideal customer.
You can use first-party data to glean key insights about your customers, tailor content to their preferences, predict their behavior and more. Squeeze every drop of value from this pot of gold and handle it as if your success depends on it — because it just might.
2. Use machine learning for paid media.
Speaking of first-party data, one of the main challenges is how to make sense of it all. Why have your staff sift through and analyze mountains of data when AI-powered solutions can do it in a fraction of the time? This is where machine learning comes in.
Simply put, machine learning is the application of artificial intelligence (AI) to help systems learn without explicit human intervention (i.e., programming). It can help you determine when a user is most likely to click on an ad and when they’re more likely to convert on your site.
One area where machine learning is already serving paid media is Google’s “Maximize conversions” bid strategy, which uses advanced machine learning to automatically optimize bids based on historical information about your campaign and budget. No more guessing games when it comes to setting bids on individual keywords.
It’s time to ditch the spreadsheets and tap into the power of machine learning for paid media (and more).
3. Focus on personalization.
We all like to feel special, and research shows that customers who get a tailored, curated experience are more likely to make a purchase. They’re also more likely to buy from you again. Two in three (66%) customers expect companies to understand their unique needs and expectations. Around the same number (68%) expect brands to demonstrate empathy.
Given these expectations, how can you deliver a more personalized customer experience? The needs of your shoppers will depend on where they are on the customer journey, of course, but here are some ideas:
• Welcome returning customers back to your site with unique images and messaging.
• Use dynamic remarketing to reach customers who are still on the fence about a purchase.
• Personalize your outreach based on specific actions, such as an abandoned cart.
• Segment your email list by things like browsing history, prior purchases, location, purchase time and other data points.
• Personalize email content with images and descriptions of products that your customers have searched for or purchased in the past.
These and other personalization tactics can help you win over customers and build brand loyalty.
4. Prioritize customer privacy.
Nearly 80% of Americans are concerned about how their data is being used by companies — and Big Tech is responding (by banning third-party cookies, for example).
Online privacy measures may be a thorn in the side of brands, but it’s what consumers are demanding. Brands will need to adapt and find new ways to predict what customers will buy without collecting personally identifiable information.
Homing in on first-party data will be crucial. Contextual targeting (display ads that are directly relevant to the product being sold) is another strategy. Also consider offering customers discounts in exchange for personal data — just know they’re likely to expect a higher level of customer service in return.
5. Command attention with TikTok and Reels.
It’s not news that video has been driving engagement for years. But short-form and bite-sized video content now dominate the social media landscape. TikTok, Instagram Reels and even YouTube Shorts are prime placement for fresh brand content. While younger audiences have traditionally been the prime target, data shows older demographics are quickly catching up.
Choose the platform that’s most likely to reach your customers. TikTok attracts a younger audience (nearly half of the platform’s users are under age 30). Instagram has a more diverse audience, with nearly half of all users falling between the ages of 25 and 44. It should be mentioned that YouTube is muscling its way into this segment with the introduction of YouTube Shorts in 2021, but user metrics specifically surrounding YouTube Shorts are still trickling in. Consider which platform is more likely to resonate with your target audience and get creating!
No matter your brand, product or business model, one of the preceding tactics is sure to set you apart from the competition. Not every brand online knocks each strategy out of the park every time, so don’t try to do everything at once. Whether you are expanding your e-commerce reach in 2022 or just getting ready to launch your new business, choose a few strategies and apply them well. Cheers to 2022!

title: Council Post: How Technology Will Revolutionize Marketing In 2022 And Beyond
text:
Founder, Digital Day.
Remember those days when you were compelled to watch TV ads just to see your favorite show? There was no “skip ads” option, and people seemed to be more patient. To address the demands of today’s customers, technology has drastically changed the shape of everything. Today, we have TVs in the palms of our hands, and we can go anywhere and have any experience while staying at home.
In the same way, technology is also revolutionizing marketing, which can be considered the key to the success of most businesses. When digital marketing was first being shaped, many overlooked its importance and continued their traditional marketing. But soon, everyone realized that online presence and reputation are indispensable. Traditional marketing still has its place, but digital marketing and technology in marketing altered everything. Today, it is your website, application or e-commerce store in front of the world representing your business and its values. This would have not been possible without modern technology.
Nonetheless, many of my fellow marketers are curious and worried about the upcoming trends we’re seeing in marketing and the fast-paced evolution of technology. How will artificial intelligence change marketing in 2022 and beyond? What will be the new technologies to spice up marketing? How will they alter marketing? Let’s take a look at some of the important technological developments that are expected to revolutionize marketing in the coming years.
Artificial Intelligence
We all know how AI is contributing to marketing by helping businesses collect user data and deliver ads and suggestions to users with similar interests. Many consumers have privacy concerns related to AI and data collection, but AI is just helping many businesses market more effectively by providing audiences with content that aligns with their interests. It is essential for brands to master the consumer persona and have a firm grasp on who their target audience is to provide customers with what they want.
The AI market is growing rapidly. In 2020, the global AI market was worth $51 billion, and it is predicted to reach $641 billion by 2028. From creating content, to powering chatbots that answer customer queries, to identifying consumer behaviors, AI is evolving to automate more and more processes.
The Metaverse
When Facebook became Meta in October, the company took the next big step into the metaverse — a connected virtual world for social connection and interaction via the internet and augmented and virtual reality headsets.
Like other technologies that didn’t seem that important at first, the metaverse will likely transform marketing. It’s only in its initial stages right now, but the metaverse is coming. No one knows how big it will be, but not preparing for it is a huge mistake.
Many big brands, such as Nike and Adidas, have already started exploring the concept of the metaverse. Both of these companies have started their work on virtual shoes.
VR And AR
Virtual reality is the simulation of objects in a 3D interactive environment to give users an immersive experience. Augmented reality is enhancing real-world objects using visuals, sounds or other sensory stimuli.
AR technology has already taken its place in the market, with many furniture stores developing mobile apps that use the technology to allow customers to place furniture into a room via mobile camera and see whether it fits or not. Indeed, this is a great convenience for customers and businesses. Other kinds of brands are using the technology as well — Gucci’s app, for example, enables users to try on shoes virtually.
While not quite mainstream yet — likely due to cost and poor user experience — VR has the potential to be an effective way of marketing as it lets you experience things whether they exist in real life or not. You can enable customers to experience your products and services without even buying them. You can use VR to take customers on a tour of stores or showrooms for an immersive experience.
Web 3.0
While Web 2.0 is still the current version of the internet as we know it, Web 3.0 has the potential to transform businesses. Technologies associated with Web 3.0 include cryptocurrency, the blockchain, non-fungible tokens and decentralized autonomous organizations. I believe that decentralization is the magic of Web 3.0 that will enable businesses and users to store and access information from all over the world simultaneously, unlike Web 2.0.
Web 3.0 could revolutionize marketing as well — it will likely be more than social media or SEO marketing. It could enhance the user experience more than ever and help marketers produce even more immersive content. How? With Web 3.0 focusing heavily on AI and natural language processing, computers will be able to understand humans better to provide better search results. And combining Web 3.0 with the metaverse will allow marketers to create highly intriguing and immersive content for advertising and communicating.
Technology is indeed revolutionizing the world for the better, and those who leverage it will be the successful ones, while the rest may suffer. New technologies such as Web 3.0 will help marketers and businesses decentralize their processes, and this will help them to break silos, conduct fast and secure transactions, and improve their customer relationships. Technology is never going to stop evolving — it will continue to transform marketing. Now and in the future, the key to success for most businesses is getting ready for this revolution.

title: A Plan For Healthcare’s Labor Shortage
text:
The healthcare labor market is facing unprecedented projected shortages across a range of specialties and services as the exodus of exhausted and depleted care workers continues.
Before, we worried about the physician shortage brought on by “normal” burnout, but pandemic burnout raises the stakes considerably and has brought an even harsher reality. Now, the majority of nurses are considering leaving the field and about one in three healthcare workers overall have considered quitting their jobs. Without major, systemic change, the healthcare industry is facing a dangerous chapter and healthcare leaders are sounding the alarm.
That systemic change should focus on two pillars to avoid a catastrophic loss of talent: making healthcare a safer, more appealing profession for people to work in and, modernizing healthcare technology to mitigate waste and inefficiencies. Since the onset of the pandemic, innovation in medicine and technology has provided numerous lifelines to keep the healthcare system functioning – we launched telehealth platforms nearly overnight, developed multiple effective vaccines in record time, and built countless patient portals and applications to accommodate demand for testing and vaccinations. Now, it’s imperative to place an emphasis on improving the working conditions for people in healthcare, in addition to advancing the technology they use.
Taking Care Of Our Healthcare Providers And Physicians
Retaining the physicians we have and attracting young people to the field starts with offering a competitive salary. Unfortunately, about half of the physicians in the U.S. feel undercompensated for their work. Doctors make a higher income relative to many industries, but consider that their work is extremely demanding and often begins with a tremendous load of debt from medical school.
Healthcare also suffers from unequal pay related to gender. A survey in Health Affairs found female physicians earned about $2 million less than male counterparts over the course of their career. Attracting young, diverse talent to medicine is growing increasingly difficult when other fields offer more competitive salaries without the prerequisite four years of medical school.
Federal agencies also have a major hand in keeping physician-owned clinics financially viable. For the first time in nearly 20 years, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has updated its rules for clinical labor pricing. The new rules took effect on January 1, 2022 and increased reimbursement from Medicare and Medicaid, taking into account the costs of employing clinical staff such as nurses and medical assistants. The new rule could not come soon enough as many independent clinics have struggled to survive the ebbs and flows of the pandemic and compensate their staff fairly.
AI Tech Built For The Practitioner
Well before the pandemic, artificial intelligence attracted significant interest from venture capital buoyed by its promise as a diagnostic tool in radiology and cancer care, among other specialties. The National Institutes of Health has also sought to harness the power of AI in diagnosing Covid-19.
While AI can never replace physicians or care providers, it can augment healthcare delivery in several key areas. Those include clinical applications such as diagnostics, and operational applications such as appointment scheduling and patient engagement. By streamlining those tasks and easing administrative burden, AI platforms will optimize the time of physicians and clinical staff. They will also make it easier to function with a reduced number of people – which may be a permanent reality for some clinics that have lost staff during the pandemic.
Particularly in diagnostics, AI has shown potential to create “physician extenders” – care team members beyond the physician who can participate in the screening of diseases accurately. In dermatology, for instance, if a nurse practitioner can evaluate an AI-enabled screening that has diagnosed skin cancer, it streamlines the process and allows the patient to start treatment as soon as possible. AI-enabled diagnostics can also triage patients and direct them to the appropriate level of care more efficiently – a critically important task as ICUs and emergency departments strain to treat patients.
Also, part of the equation that has ballooned the cost of healthcare in the U.S. can be traced to unnecessary expenses, such as duplicative testing. Realizing AI’s full potential and eliminating the variable of human error in diagnostics will significantly reduce the incidence of unnecessary testing and reduce healthcare costs.
AI can also unlock the value of big data from a healthcare perspective. In the hands of physicians and researchers, machine learning applied to healthcare data can accelerate detection of diseases, drug discovery, and eventual treatments. Scientists around the world had free access to the SARS-CoV-2 genome by January of 2020 and that level of information sharing dramatically accelerated the timeline for developing diagnostic tests and therapies to treat and prevent Covid-19. It showed the value of data sharing in the most urgent time of need and the value of a shared clinical database that can save physicians precious time in research.
By augmenting both clinical and operational capabilities, AI will elevate the work experience in medicine to something that more closely resembles other modern industries with highly sophisticated technology. AI integrations will also make it more appealing for entrepreneurial physicians to own and operate their own clinic without burdening them with all the work traditionally associated with billing and revenue cycle management.
The race to retain and attract new talent in healthcare is coming to a crescendo, but emerging technologies and an emphasis on improving conditions for physicians and healthcare providers will help to mitigate the impending shortage. In the same way the industry pushed for rapid adoption of telehealth, and developed vaccines at breakneck speed, we need to support our healthcare workers and push for tech-enabled environments in the healthcare ecosystem. A modernized work experience will help to attract new talent to the field while helping to retain the healthcare workers we already have. Healthcare has to confront the reality of a shortage of care providers by ensuring competitive salaries and fair reimbursements for the work of physicians and clinical staff.
By supporting our clinicians and enhancing their work with the right technologies, we can avoid the worst-case scenarios of a labor shortage in healthcare.

title: Strict Literal Interpretation Is A Hardheaded Drawback Of Machine Learning And Likewise Bad For AI Self-Driving Cars
text:
Here’s an interesting thought experiment.
Pretend that you took all words at their literal interpretation, all of the time, wherever you went, and acted upon those words strictly and accordingly.
For example, suppose you are driving in your car and perchance see a billboard that is touting the message that you should eat at Joe’s Pizzeria, accessible at the next exit up ahead. The normal course of events would be that you would consult your stomach to ascertain whether you are hungry. Furthermore, if you were hungry, the next question is whether you want pizza. Upon deciding that maybe you do want pizza, the next aspect would be whether you want to take the upcoming exit and eat at Joe’s Pizzeria since you might have in mind some other pizza eatery instead.
But, none of those sensible and reasonable ideas rattle around in your noggin.
We have agreed that you are going to take everything in a meticulously literal way. By gosh, the billboard instructed you to go eat at Joe’s Pizzeria, so that’s what you are going to do. Come heck or high water, you will take the next exit and you will drive straight to that pizzeria and you will order yourself a juicy hot pizza.
This might work out okay and you’ll be happy that you obediently abided by the wording of the billboard. Perhaps though this side trip has made you late for work. Your boss won’t especially appreciate that you opted to be tardy because you just had to get a slice of pizza. Ouch, your boss fires you the moment you proffer such a lame excuse.
Turns out that you don’t even like pizza.
It causes your stomach to churn and you had to swear off pizza a few years ago. Why did you go eat pizza? A dumb thing to do. Anyway, since you are stridently taking everything at its word, the billboard said to go eat the pizza and you complied. You achieved the literal interpretation credo to an unerring degree.
I think it safe to say that we would be surprised to find any sentient human that would act in this manner.
One supposes that perhaps a person could be hypnotized into this kind of mental state, maybe. Or a person might voluntarily try to take everything in a literal fashion, though this is unlikely to be fulfillable.
You are bound to come across sentences and words that get you boxed up.
Take as an example the everyday stop sign that you see while driving your car.
Depending upon how far you want to take things, the word “STOP” indicates you are to come to a stop. There isn’t another word there that says to go ahead and go. As such, if you strictly abide by a stop sign, you would come to a stop and sit tight. Unless or until you saw some other wording that suggested otherwise, you would remain in that halted position.
I guess you could stay there as long as you wanted, at least until another car came up behind you and got so disgusted with your sitting still that the driver erupted into road rage or decided to steamily summon the police.
In this imaginary scenario, you simply saw the word “stop” and that was sufficient to get you to bring your car to a halt. We can slightly recast things and contemplate that you will at least first visually examine the stop message and only come to an actual stop if the signage sufficiently resembles a proper standardized stop sign.
I mean by this that the sign says STOP in all capitals. This appears as white letters on a red background. The sign is in an octagon shape. It is mounted on a pole. Those are the customary characteristics that you would see in the United States.
The good news is that you aren’t going to construe a store named Stop-n-Go or StopMart as being a stop sign. You’ll readily drive right past those establishments and not feel compelled to stop at either one. Thus, the indication of the word “stop” in that other format or labeling is insufficient to trigger your literal interpretation mindset.
Why all this discussion and angst about literal interpretation?
You might be thinking that this is a tempest in a teapot. There would never be a circumstance of this kind of literal interpretation going on. All in all, the whole shebang seems overly contrived and nothing more than a silly exercise in silliness.
Au contraire, mon ami (on the contrary, my friends)!
Here’s the deal.
Let’s discuss self-driving cars (for my ongoing and extensive coverage of Autonomous Vehicles or AVs, including self-driving cars, see the link here).
The advent of today’s self-driving cars relies upon the use of image processing as a key element in ascertaining the driving scene. Video cameras are mounted onto self-driving cars and the video is real-time streamed into an image processing computer system onboard the vehicle. The software of the image processing system takes the collected imagery and tries to figure out what objects might be found in the video being collected.
One especially crucial intent is to discover whether other cars are nearby to the self-driving car. Maybe there is a car directly ahead and another car to the immediate left of the driverless vehicle. Indeed, a slew of objects is potentially within visual range. Besides finding the images of cars, the software is likely trying to spot any nearby pedestrians, any nearby animals that might be on the loose, and so on.
A common means these days of doing this type of image processing consists of using AI-based techniques and technologies such as Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL). Those capabilities are neither magical and nor sentient. They are simply souped-up computational pattern matching algorithms.
The way that they work entails first “training” the ML/DL algorithms on data that you have previously put together or obtained, and which suitably reflects whatever kinds of objects you are hoping the ML/DL can find. For example, you might establish an extensive database of images depicting various makes and models of cars. Those are fed into the ML/DL. The ML/DL mathematically tries to identify the contours and characteristics associated with those various cars.
If you do things well, the ML/DL can be somewhat generalizable as to attempting to spot a car within a captured image. Suppose though that you only fed into the ML/DL during training a set of cars that were all of one specific make and model. The chances are that this would make things confounding when trying to use the ML/DL on any everyday roadway.
Video streaming would be bringing in the images of a wide variety of cars, and yet the ML/DL might only be declaring that some of those objects are in fact cars. The rest of those objects are either not declarable and considered to be unknown or they might get assigned a probability that they maybe might be a car though the certainty is very low (the uncertainty is stated as high).
In addition to trying to get the ML/DL to find cars in an image, you would also seek to have the AI capabilities to find various traffic signs. This would consist of first establishing a database of traffic signs and use those during an ML/DL training stage. After doing that, you then would place the ML/DL devised image processing software into a self-driving car. Consequently, the image processing will attempt to computationally match the objects in the everyday video imagery to the prior trained semblance of what traffic signs look like.
This brings us to the revered and vaunted STOP sign.
You would undoubtedly assume that training the computational pattern matching about the look of a classic STOP sign would be a piece of cake. There are visually apparent capital letters, those distinctive colors of the sign, and the readily recognizable octogen shape, all amounting to some pretty definitive telltale clues.
Easy-peasy.
Aha, caught you again!
In the real world, a stop sign might be partially obscured due to a tree that overhangs the sign. If the ML/DL is mathematically construing that a STOP sign has to entirely showcase the word “stop” and do so without any discrepancies, it might mark that the object detected was not rated at all or is unable to be classified as a stop sign (or might be assigned a low probability).
Humans would be unlikely to make such a mistake in identification. We all have seen plenty of such stop signs that were only partially fully visible and yet nonetheless could classify them as valid stop signs. Go ahead and pat yourself on the back for being a human, and one that can usually discern a stop sign. See, you can do things that might seem extraordinary.
Back to the drawing board, we might want to do some retaining as it were and feed into the ML/DL a bunch of images of stop signs that are partially obscured with trees and large-sized bushes. The computational pattern matching would now be calculated to potentially include the facet of a partially obscured stop sign.
Suppose you are driving along and there is a stop sign up ahead, but it is partially obscured because a quite tall person is standing next to the sign. The towering person is wearing a tall hat. Only about one-third of the stop sign is visible. Do you think that you would still be able to discern that this was a valid stop sign?
I’d claim that you likely could.
Would the ML/DL that was computationally trained via those stop signs that were partially obscured by trees and bushes be able to spot the stop sign?
Maybe yes, maybe no.
You see, it is conceivable that the pictures of the trees and bushes overhanging the signs had become integral to the calculations in ascertaining what a stop sign looks like. If a stop sign has green things that are leafy and partially obscuring the stop sign, it is likely to be a stop sign. If a stop is fully visible, it is likely to be a stop sign. Anything else, such as a stop sign being blocked somewhat by a tall person with a tall hat, well, that’s not presumably a stop sign.
You could lay this at the feet of literal interpretation.
Unlike humans that can go beyond literal interpretation, the ML/DL of today’s measure is extremely limited and considered altogether brittle. The computational pattern matching is apt to land on aspects of the imagery that a human would not be so confounded by. You would realize that if leaves and trees can block part of a stop sign, so can a lot of other things. As such, you would mentally refine your thinking that any partial image of a stop sign could be a stop sign, and you need to take into account a variety of contextual elements to reach a deliberated decision about it.
That is not something that today’s AI systems are able to readily do. There is a monkey-see-monkey-do sense of what the ML/DL is doing, though even that is an overstatement since a monkey has a semblance of sentience that none of today’s AI does (put your money on the monkey winning over contemporary AI in an open-ended task).
This brings up an important question: Does this troublesome problem of literal interpretation bode for issues about the advent of AI-based true self-driving cars?
Before jumping into the details, I’d like to clarify what is meant when referring to true self-driving cars.
Understanding The Levels Of Self-Driving Cars
As a clarification, true self-driving cars are ones that the AI drives the car entirely on its own and there isn’t any human assistance during the driving task.
These driverless vehicles are considered Level 4 and Level 5 (see my explanation at this link here), while a car that requires a human driver to co-share the driving effort is usually considered at Level 2 or Level 3. The cars that co-share the driving task are described as being semi-autonomous, and typically contain a variety of automated add-on’s that are referred to as ADAS (Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems).
There is not yet a true self-driving car at Level 5, which we don’t yet even know if this will be possible to achieve, and nor how long it will take to get there.
Meanwhile, the Level 4 efforts are gradually trying to get some traction by undergoing very narrow and selective public roadway trials, though there is controversy over whether this testing should be allowed per se (we are all life-or-death guinea pigs in an experiment taking place on our highways and byways, some contend, see my coverage at this link here).
Since semi-autonomous cars require a human driver, the adoption of those types of cars won’t be markedly different than driving conventional vehicles, so there’s not much new per se to cover about them on this topic (though, as you’ll see in a moment, the points next made are generally applicable).
For semi-autonomous cars, it is important that the public needs to be forewarned about a disturbing aspect that’s been arising lately, namely that despite those human drivers that keep posting videos of themselves falling asleep at the wheel of a Level 2 or Level 3 car, we all need to avoid being misled into believing that the driver can take away their attention from the driving task while driving a semi-autonomous car.
You are the responsible party for the driving actions of the vehicle, regardless of how much automation might be tossed into a Level 2 or Level 3.
Self-Driving Cars And Literal Interpretation
For Level 4 and Level 5 true self-driving vehicles, there won’t be a human driver involved in the driving task.
All occupants will be passengers.
The AI is doing the driving.
One aspect to immediately discuss entails the fact that the AI involved in today’s AI driving systems is not sentient. In other words, the AI is altogether a collective of computer-based programming and algorithms, and most assuredly not able to reason in the same manner that humans can (see my analysis at this link here).
Why this added emphasis about the AI not being sentient?
Because I want to underscore that when discussing the role of the AI driving system, I am not ascribing human qualities to the AI. Please be aware that there is an ongoing and dangerous tendency these days to anthropomorphize AI. In essence, people are assigning human-like sentience to today’s AI, despite the undeniable and inarguable fact that no such AI exists as yet.
With that clarification, you can envision that the AI driving system won’t natively somehow “know” about the facets of driving. Driving and all that it entails will need to be programmed as part of the hardware and software of the self-driving car.
Let’s dive into the myriad of aspects that come to play on this topic.
We will continue with the stop sign exemplar as a means of digging deeper into the existing limitations of AI techniques such as Machine Learning and Deep Learning. Realize that the stop sign is only a microcosm and the gist herein is aiming to reveal a larger macroscopic revelation.
For those of you keenly interested in the specifics of stop signs, you might relish taking a look at the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) published by the U.S. Department of Transportation (US DOT) under the auspices of the Federal Highway Administration (FHA). According to this official standard, a STOP sign must be an octagonal shape consisting of a white legend and a border on a red background. There are lots of other characteristics, but I think we all pretty much are familiar with such signs and know them when we see them.
Now for a bit of a saga on the topic.
A team that was preparing part of an AI driving system had sought to develop an image processing component that would recognize stop signs. They were able to obtain a database of images that encompassed stop signs. These were primarily close-ups of stop signs, whereby the stop sign took up most of the picture and there was a clear-cut focus on the stop sign (versus, for example, if these were images that perchance had stop signs somewhere in the image and that might have varied substantially in how well the stop sign could be readily spotted).
The AI developers used a topnotch ML/DL to do computational pattern matching on the database of stop sign images. As is commonly undertaken in such efforts, they held back a portion of the database to be used as a test set. Thus, you first do the “training” of the ML/DL via the preponderance of the dataset, and then you afterward try to ascertain the veracity of the derived pattern matching, doing so by using the smaller set-aside portion for testing purposes. The resulting ML/DL did quite well on the test set and achieved extremely high marks for being able to ferret out the images of stop signs.
There was a lot of congratulatory backslapping and high-fiving about how good the ML/DL was at finding stop signs. They then opted to make use of the stop sign finder in field tests on real-world roads.
This consisted of having the self-driving car drive around an area and see how well the stop sign detection functioned. To their unpleasant surprise, there were quite a number of misses such that the image processing was not signifying stop signs that undisputedly did exist. Meanwhile, the human backup driver present in the vehicle was able to readily see those missed stop signs and opted to momentarily take over the driving controls due to the AI ML/DL oversights.
What was going on inside the ML/DL that was leading to these lapses?
Well, as a heads-up, one ongoing qualm about most of today’s ML/DL is that there is no easy way to get the pattern matching to somehow explain what is going on (see my discussion about XAI or explanatory AI at this link here). Essentially, the mathematics underlying ML/DL pattern matching is typically rather arcane and not readily interpretable in any everyday logical means. You have no immediate way of figuring out why the system was detecting stop signs properly some of the time and at other times not seemingly doing so.
The AI developers decided to study closely the images of the stop signs that were being missed or skipped (i.e., a stop sign that was not being classified as a stop sign by the ML/DL). They had a bit of a head-scratcher after poking around and trying to figure out what was going on. Finally, they figured out the matter.
Here’s the reveal.
When you or I look at a stop sign, we see the word “STOP” in caps, we see the white colors of the letters, we see the red color of the background, and we see the octogen shape. That’s sufficient for us to decide that a stop sign is a stop sign.
Keeping in mind that stop signs are customarily mounted on poles, there is something else there that you might not normally notice. Usually, a stop sign is affixed to a pole via the use of two bolts. There is a bolt toward the top of the sign and another bolt toward the bottom of the sign. These are typically head bolts or sometimes corner bolts. In any case, they are there to keep the sign on the pole.
Look closely next time while driving and you’ll notice the bolts (but keep your eyes on the road, please!).
When the ML/DL was doing the computational pattern matching, a characteristic of the stop signs was that they all had those two bolts. Furthermore, the bolts were, all the same, just a normal bolt with a normal bolt head. They were also always placed above and below the word “STOP” on the sign. This is perhaps obvious as I tell you about it, but if you asked most people about what a stop sign looks like, I’d dare say that few would right away mention the bolts.
If you saw a stop sign that did not have those bolts, would you still recognize the stop sign as a stop sign?
I’d think you would.
For example, you come upon a construction zone and a worker is holding up a stop sign that is affixed to a wooden post resembling a paddle. There might not be any bolts on this stop sign, or they might be hidden from the front of the stop sign. You would still realize that this is a valid stop sign and you would recognize it as such.
The ML/DL mathematically calculated that stop signs must include two boltheads. That was computationally decreed as an essential ingredient of a stop sign. This makes sense because the provided set of stop signs all had that feature.
If the only scrutiny is one of a considered literal interpretation, it seems appropriate to ascertain that all stop signs have those two bolts.
Guess what.
Of the stop signs that weren’t being detected, they all had some subtle differences about the bolts.
For example, there were some of the encountered stop signs that had washers just beneath the boltheads, which is a prudently added aspect, though not necessarily needed and often not included. The original dataset used for training and testing did not have any such instances. The aspect of an added washer was confounding the pattern matching probability being assigned by the ML/DL because the stop sign looked different than it was supposed to look.
There was a stop sign that was missing the bottom bolt entirely (the stop sign needed repair in the sense that a bolt was supposed to be present). The fact that there wasn’t a bolt where it was supposed to be was again reducing the assigned probability by the ML/DL pattern matching.
I don’t want to belabor the point, and the AI developers were able to rerun the ML/DL with a revised set of stop signs that included a wider variety of circumstances, ergo you could suggest that this was “easily solved” in a manner of speaking.
The emphasis herein is that this was a variant of the literal interpretation problem.
Conclusion
AI systems of today do not have any semblance of common-sense reasoning.
Human drivers make use of common sense when they see STOP signs that aren’t precisely what a stop sign is supposed to look like. The mind of a human driver considers the overall context and driving situation to make a reasoned decision about all facets of driving, including detecting the humble but ever so crucial stop sign.
Some believe that we will not be able to attain true self-driving cars until we have figured out how to embed common-sense reasoning into AI technologies. Without that capability, there will be an infinite number of loopholes or edge cases that are going to confound any AI driving system.
As was perhaps evident, not detecting a stop sign is a bad thing.
Luckily, a human backup driver was involved in those driving efforts and kept the self-driving car from running a stop sign. Had the self-driving car rushed past a stop sign, heaven knows what could have occurred if a human-driven car was proceeding along or a pedestrian stepped suddenly into the street due to the assumption that the autonomous vehicle was going to properly come to a halt.
There is the matter too of detecting a stop sign for which it is not relevant to the driving task at hand. You might be puzzled at how this might occur. A classic example consists of billboards that have what looks like a stop sign as part of the billboard ad, using the iconic image to catch the attention of human drivers. Human drivers instantly realize that the stop sign isn’t something to be abided with and is simply part of a display ad.
Self-driving cars passing the billboard mistakenly construed the ad as though it was an actual stop sign to be obeyed. This can be bad if the AI driving system brings the vehicle to a stop when there is no needed basis to do so. There are numerous cases of stop signs being detected that were irrelevant to the existing path of a self-driving car (I’ve written about such instances).
All told, we’ve got to get past the limitations of literal interpretation if we are going to increasingly rely on AI and hang onto those heightened expectations for what AI can achieve.
And I mean that, literally.

title: How The Path From Digital Automation To Autonomy Will Disrupt Enterprise In 2022
text:
Every significant technology disruption has led to fundamental changes in how businesses are run, what products and services are sold, and how customers engage with enterprises. Personal computers and the Internet propelled new business models and value chains, while smartphones and cloud computing enabled a shift toward more mobile, on-demand services.
Technology also enabled us as humans to connect in new ways, often with little or no regard for our differences in a physical location. We are on the cusp of another era of disruption, based on artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning and robotic process automation (RPA) that promises to reshape further the nature of work and how we collaborate.
Each technology wave has brought tremendous opportunity to those who understand how to leverage these new capabilities. This time around is no different: businesses that master this digitization trend will better serve customers, lower costs and drive revenue.
As digital technology infiltrates every corner of the business, companies must shift focus from simply automating existing processes to fully digitizing their operations and elevating the role of the Chief Digital Officer. That means not only transforming how they engage with customers but also fundamentally changing the way they operate internally by adopting new technologies that help employees work more effectively and collaboratively.
Natural language processing, Computer vision, AI engineering, Autonomic Systems, Generative AI, and workforce augmentation are some of the new trends Gartner emphasized. Those technologies help make sense of information generated by employees, customers, machines and things to support better decision-making across industries. The IoT makes it possible to connect physical objects into the digital world through embedded sensors that allow real-time operations visibility. Mobile and wearable devices enable workers and customers to communicate and transact anytime, anywhere.
These disruptive technologies can help companies acquire and retain customers, create new business models and drive revenue growth — but only if they are implemented correctly. Businesses need systems that connect across internal functions and the customer experience. They need solutions that collaborate with other enterprise applications to provide the correct information to the right people at the right time. And they need security that can keep up with employees' increasing demands for mobility and collaboration. This article will create a roadmap at how end-to-end digital automation and autonomy bring together business strategy, scalable operating models and the right mix of tools and technologies to help companies achieve impact with digital transformation.
Extreme Customer Experience
Customers no longer tolerate substandard or cookie-cutter services. They desire intuitive, seamless, and personal interactions. This is where integration and orchestration come in handy.
This next generation of automation uses machine learning and data science tools to deliver extreme personalization and customer experiences. It provides conversational interfaces powered by advanced knowledge graphs, text-to-speech and deep learning systems.
According to the CEO of the Everest Group, Peter Bendor-Samuel, “ Automating a process is the most cost-effective approach to labor and yields the maximum amount of savings. Implementing a Voice Response Unit (VRU) system is at the heart of this approach. VRUs connect to IVR (interactive voice response) systems for customers to make choices or direct a transaction. The system gives a customer a set of alternatives from which to narrow down the reason for the call so the system can funnel the customer to the right person in the company.”
Moreover, Virtual Assistants (VA) like Amazon's Alexa, Google Assistant, or Microsoft Cortana are taking center stage in this new world where customer experience is everything. They make interactions more straightforward and personalized through intelligent, context-sensitive interactions.
Business Leaders are responsible for Transformation Leaders Are in Charge.
Previously, IIT leaders CIOs and IT departments handled routine automation, eventually implemented in other business units areas. The invention of low-code development platforms that don't require heavy programming knowledge has revolutionized how automation is implemented.
Business leaders can now use automation to build multi-disciplinary and multi-stakeholder cross-functional teams that can turn data into insight and action at speed by partnering with us. Business leaders always link their investments to business value creation back to business advantages — they understand how automation will benefit all stakeholders of an organization, including its consumers and staff.
It's also essential that an organization has sound execution capabilities and the ability to change rapidly — which we refer to as "agility." Open-source frameworks like Agile, Cloud Foundry and Microservices are part of hyper-agility trends.
Lastly, CDOs, CIOs and business leaders can use advanced automation tools to create repeatable, agile architectural models. According to CDO Trends, Data Enrichment is at the top of many CIO's priority lists for two reasons: The first is that it takes human beings out of the data acquisition process. This leads to the second reason: increasing automation increases accuracy and speed. "When enrichment data is combined with source system data, the resulting data model can now include a complete picture of the data being mastered as seen by a subject matter expert. Enrichment data make sure you have enough data for effective mastering."
As an organization builds capabilities with the help of CDOs, CIOs and IT leaders, those organizations must have a solid foundation to initiate from which they can support those new initiatives. The essential function of enterprise architecture (EA) is to provide a blueprint of the critical importance of the technical and organizational components necessary to support business strategy and deliver value to customers and other stakeholders.
An organization must have sound execution capabilities; it also needs the ability to change rapidly — which we refer to as "agility." Open-source frameworks like Agile, Cloud Foundry, and Microservices are all part of this trend toward hyper-agility.
Managing Talent Retention
Talent management has become a key differentiator for enterprises. All of this needs to be supported and will need to be backed by world-class recruiting and retention approaches and strategies that foster subject matter expertise, diversity, inclusivity, and lifelong learning culture. The market has never been more competitive for people with Digital and AI skillset, and this trend is likely to continue for many years.
Automation accelerates employee happiness by allowing them to devote more time to higher-value collaborative and creative activities. Employees are more willing to stick around and assist in recruiting future talent when they feel recognized and supported.
Hyper automation
Hyper automation is the process of automating the entire business ecosystem, with collaboration between machines and humans. This platform focuses on driving operational excellence with digital technologies like robotics process automation (RPA)artificial intelligence (AI).
Executives should stop seeing automation as composed of siloed units and independent elements. Instead, automation technologies become pieces of the same puzzle that different areas of the enterprise leverage at the same time. Moreover, as digital technologies such as AI and RPA continue to mature, we'll see more intelligent automation — or "hyper-automation" — that provides context around the tasks being completed. It's a business-driven framework for businesses and IT to identify, vet, and automate enterprise operations as possible.
By 2025, Gartner expects the market for this software to be worth nearly $860 billion. Hype automation will remain the driving force behind digital transformation in 2022 to increase accuracy and productivity.
AI will lead the way to hyper-automation, which involves many automated activities. Some of these activities include
- Process mining
- Robotic process automation (RPA)
- Low-code workflow platforms
- Intelligent agents
