- Artificial intelligence (AI)
For example, American Fidelity, an insurance firm, has discovered tremendous time savings thanks to UiPath's RPA solutions despite some early resistance. Employees were encouraged to playfully utilize the project slogan "Drop the Drudgery" to recognize that they could use RPA to complete tasks they probably didn't want to do in the first place. Employees used to read each email, tag it, and route it to the correct channel by hand, but thanks to RPA and machine learning, processing speeds were reduced from 45 hours to 3 seconds.
In addition, according to the CIO Magazine, “RPA is also replacing grunt work at immigration law firm Berry Appleman & Leiden LLP, which has seen a sharp uptick in business thanks to tech clients scrambling to hire staff on H-1B visas. The firm uses UiPath’s software to collect information, including wage data, as well as resumes and passports, from government websites such as the U.S. Bureau of Labor and enter it into its case management platform, Vince DiMascio, the firm’s CIO, told CIO.com at the MIT Sloan CIO Symposium in May.”
Agility Matters
To stay ahead of the curve, leaders must pick the proper AI/machine learning tools pre-trained to deliver a return on investment to stay ahead of the curve. Working with a partner with success stories and case studies that were successfully used is a way to expedite the procedure.
To stay competitive, businesses must move fast. Enterprise officials may begin by assessing their automation maturity to ensure that the company automates intelligently and appropriately for their enterprise.
For example, it's essential to know where automation can have the most significant impact instead of automating every process. By prioritizing processes for automation, organizations can gain a better return on their investment while delivering better customer experiences at the same time.
Data Fabric
A data fabric is a network of linked data sources connected to business objectives and KPIs, and it may be used to provide critical insights throughout the organization. According to MarketWatch, this market is anticipated to expand by more than 25% by 2025.
For example, “The MapR Data Management platform example, binds together “real-time, dead, and batch” data for collective analysis. The MapR data fabric enables the user to grant access to both existing applications or tools and new tools like Apache Drill. This platform enables access to “data in all forms” across “all locations.” The basic objective of MapR data fabric is to break down data silos for just-in-time access to all types of data,” according to The Modern Data Fabric — What It Means to Your Business.
Not only is data fabric highly flexible and scalable, but it's also adaptable to more sophisticated applications. Machine learning (ML) models in data fabric systems allow better accessibility of the prepared data across models and applications while reducing data preparation time. Data fabric provisions “controlled access” to secure data, allowing for more efficient ML procedures when data is dispersed across an organization — on the cloud, on-premise, or at the Edge (IoT). When the proper data is fed to ML models at the right time, they can learn much more effectively.
AI in Metaverse
In 2022, many enterprises will begin to use AI-driven applications in the metaverse. The metaverse is defined as an immersive, networked, 3D, virtual environment where people can socialize and access information. This exciting area includes virtual worlds and augmented reality experiences. Meta will significantly impact next-generation automation. Instead of interacting with different systems, customers will experience a cohesive end-to-end service in the metaverse due to the full scale of integration and orchestration capabilities.
The metaverse is forcing the development of digital ecology in which various software and portals interact, engage, and collaborate in an alternative Second world. Meta will construct a single, unified online experience for customers in 2022.
For example, Meta and Microsoft are positioning themselves as leaders in the metaverse. Given that Facebook has renamed itself to reflect the metaverse trend, Meta may appear to be all-in on the metaverse phenomenon. That commitment to the subject and its Oculus Quest 2 VR headsets is proof of a more thorough dedication than simply changing names. Meanwhile, Microsoft is also focused on the metaverse, but it has made a total commitment to that end only relatively recently. Its latest purchase of Activision Blizzard shows that commitment. In the future, we can expect to see the cohesion of a digital virtual world with the proliferation of VR/AR headsets.
Edge Computing Intelligence
This is another critical trend that businesses must prepare for now.
Edge Computing intelligence in enterprises establishes closed-loop actions for managing company operations in the most optimized way. Edge computing intelligence helps continuously assess and predict potential risks in creating a solution and eliminating threats.
Essentially, edge intelligence accelerates products and services at the edge to resolve resolutions of problems faster. This particular integration helps eliminate the usage of third-party tools.
The Way Forward
While the trends mentioned above will undoubtedly impact enterprises and businesses, they're not going to happen overnight.
Organizations must start preparing by developing the skills and competencies that their employees need to work in a digital workplace environment where AI agents and automated systems collaborate to provide customers with an exceptional end-to-end service experience.
This is expected to be a significant trend as companies must ensure that their systems operate upon the same set of accurate data. Moreover, integrating and orchestrating artificial intelligence capabilities at the edge will help eliminate third-party tools and expedite market new products.
Elevating the role of the CDO will help in this regard by providing a single point of accountability to oversee the digital transformation, including future trends in AI and automation.
As these technologies become more widely adopted, organizations should focus on developing the skills and competencies needed to work with them effectively. For example, digital learning platforms can simulate real-life scenarios and provide employees with a realistic work environment that's more cost-effective and accessible.
It's also essential for businesses to prepare by developing the necessary digital skills that their employees need to work in an environment where AI agents and automated systems collaborate to provide customers with an exceptional end-to-end service experience.

title: Under 30 Asia Alum Launches AI Startup With Funding From Kai-Fu Lee’s Sinovation Ventures And ZhenFund
text:
A Singapore-based startup that’s speeding up artificial intelligence computations through high-performance computing has attracted $4.7 million in venture capital, says founder and CEO You Yang.
Founded in August last year, the startup, HPC-AI Tech, received the funding from former Google China chief Kai-Fu Lee's Sinovation Ventures, Forbes Midas Lister Anna Fang's ZhenFund and Menlo Park-based BlueRun Ventures, according to You, a Forbes 30 Under 30 Asia alum from 2021.
The startup, which also has an office in Beijing, uses cloud-based technology to speed up central processing units and graphics processing units so both can keep up with ever faster AI models, You says. In more technical terms, his high-performance computing system (the “HPC” in the name stands for “high performance computing”) speeds up the training and inference process of AI models.
“To help more enterprises and more people to fully utilize AI, we developed this system so the user can just write the code on their laptop and our system can automatically power their AI to deploy AI to cloud or to supercomputers,” You says.
“We made HPC-AI as one of our top priority investment topics in 2021 due to two trends we discovered in AI,” says Bob Ren, an executive director at Sinovation Ventures. “The first trend is large-scale AI model. In 2020, we noticed that large-scale AI model is rapidly developing and is close to application, especially in NLP and CV. The second trend is AI for Science, which is the 4th Paradigm of science.”
“AI models mixed with simulations will change our approaches of research and development,” adds Ren. “Dr. Yang You is a top-tier scientist in HPC-AI, and has great capability of improving his technology and building a successful company to capture this opportunity.”
You says HPC-AI currently has 10 clients, including Chinese auto maker Geely. He has set a goal of 1,000 clients in three years with a 50% annual increase after that. “I think there will be a big demand in the future,” he says. Self-driving cars would especially need his technology, he adds, because their “huge” AI models require high-performance computing to run.
You points to Grid.ai and Anyscale, both based in the U.S., as competitors. He expects HPC-AI will stand out with technology that can scale AI training on a single PC up to hundreds of machines via cloud or supercomputer.
AI software revenue will total $62.5 billion this year, up 21.3% over 2021, market research firm Gartner forecasts. The high-performance computing market is expected to grow from $37.8 billion in 2020 to $49.4 billion by 2025, according to research firm MarketsandMarkets.
You got the idea for his startup through academic work coupled with inspirations from the late Steve Jobs and Tesla CEO Elon Musk. His mother ran a clothing shop when You was growing up in China, exposing him to business culture.
Before his startup launched, You and his associates had broken two world records for AI speeds. In 2019, the most recent record, he and a team claimed the top BERT training speed, which is a benchmark used by Google and Microsoft, among others, to measure a machine's understanding of human languages.
The founder received an electrical engineering-computer science Ph.D. from U.C. Berkeley between August 2015 and August 2020, and received there a Lotfi A. Zadeh Prize for AI-related work. You, 30, teaches computer science today at the National University of Singapore.

title: The 5 Technologies That Will Change The Future Of The Human Race
text:
In my book, Tech Trends in Practice, I talk about a lot of technology trends that are already moving out of the R&D departments and into everyday life, but the following five I think will have the most profound impacts on our society and the human race as a whole.
Artificial Intelligence
Artificial intelligence, or AI, and machine learning refer to the ability of machines to learn and act intelligently, meaning they can make decisions, carry out tasks, and even predict future outcomes based on what they learn from data.
AI and machine learning already play a bigger role in everyday life than you might imagine. Alexa, Siri, Amazon's product recommendations, Netflix’s and Spotify’s personalized recommendations, every Google search you make, security checks for fraudulent credit card purchases, dating apps, fitness trackers... All are driven by AI.
AI is going to revolutionize almost every facet of modern life. Stephen Hawking said, “Success in creating AI would be the biggest event in human history.” And Hawking immediately followed that up with, “Unfortunately, it might also be the last, unless we learn how to avoid the risks."
There are potentially huge risks for society and human life as we know it, particularly when you consider some countries are racing to develop AI-enabled autonomous weapons. AI and machine learning are the foundation on which many other technologies are built. For instance, without AI, we wouldn't have achieved the amazing advances in the Internet of Things, virtual reality, chatbots, facial recognition, robotics, automation, or self-driving cars, just to name a few.
AI is also going to transform human jobs. AI-enabled automation will have a particularly significant impact and may lead to the displacement of many jobs. But rather than subscribing to a vision of a dystopian future where all human jobs are given over to robots, I believe AI will make our working lives better. AI will enhance the work of humans, and new jobs will arise to replace displaced jobs.
What's more, as machines become more intelligent and capable of carrying out more human tasks, I believe that our uniquely human capabilities, things like creativity, empathy, and critical thinking, will become all the more precious and valuable in the workplaces of the future.
Gene Technology
Genomics is an interdisciplinary field of biology that focuses on the understanding and manipulation of DNA and genomes of living organisms. Gene editing is a group of technologies that enables genetic engineering in order to change the DNA and genetic structure of living organisms.
Biotechnology is advancing to the point where it's viable to alter the DNA encoded within a cell; this will influence the characteristics or traits that its descendants will have. In plants, this could affect the number of leaves or their coloring, while in humans, it could affect their height, eye color, or their likelihood of developing diseases. This opens up a range of possibilities that are almost unlimited, as it means that any characteristic of a living organism that is inherited can theoretically be changed.
Much of the work being done with gene editing is in the field of healthcare. Among the most exciting current projects is the correction of DNA mutations which can lead to serious illnesses such as cancer or heart disease. But, perhaps more than with any other technology, there are a huge number of ethical and legal concerns as well as "what if" questions when it comes to genetic manipulation and editing. Genome editing in humans is currently banned in many countries, including much of Europe, as its long-term results are not understood.
With anything as potentially transformative to society as genomics, it can be easy to get carried away thinking about possibilities such as wiping out cancer or even indefinitely prolonging human life. In reality, such huge advances are likely to be a long way away, if they are ever possible at all. Focusing on solving smaller problems that will have an immediate real-world impact is likely to be more fruitful in the short term.
Human-Computer Interfaces
Human-computer interfaces create wearable devices and technology that help to improve the physical and potentially mental performance of humans and help us lead healthier and better lives. Perhaps the most prevalent examples of wearables today are fitness tracker bands and smartwatches: small, easy to wear devices that typically monitor our activity and provide insights that help us lead healthier, better, more productive lives.
However, the term wearable doesn't necessarily mean something that you strap onto your wrist or where elsewhere on your body; it also extends to smart clothing such as running shoes that can measure your gait and performance, advances like robotic prosthetics, and robotic wearable technology used in industrial settings.
As technology gets smaller and smarter, the sheer range of wearables is going to expand, and new, smaller, smarter products will emerge to supersede the wearables we're familiar with today. For example, we already have smart glasses, but these are likely to be replaced by smart contact lenses. After that, smart contact lenses will likely be replaced by smart eye implants.
Advances like this lead many to believe that humans and machines will eventually merge to create truly augmented humans, transhumans, or humans 2.0, where the human body is souped up like a sports car to achieve enhanced physical and mental performance. This would transform the world of medicine and eventually maybe even challenge our understanding of what it means to be human.
At a societal level, we could be heading toward an even greater divide between rich and poor, between the Haves and the Have Nots. Technology is promising to help us live longer and healthier lives, maybe even offering the chance to live forever, but probably only for those who can afford it. Imagine a society in which the rich are effectively superhumans that live forever, and everyone else is normal and disadvantaged... There's also a wider ethical question about whether we should want to live exceedingly long lives given the huge strain that would put on our planet.
Extended Reality (XR)
Extended reality, or XR for short, encompasses virtual reality, augmented reality, and mixed reality and refers to the use of technology to create more immersive digital experiences.
In practice, XR is being used to boost brand engagement, let customers try before they buy, enhance customer service, make workplace learning more effective, and improve other organizational processes.
XR Technologies offer exciting and entirely new ways for people to experience the world around them. XR technology is already finding very real applications in our world, and is likely to dramatically change the way we interact with technology. In fact, mobile-based AR experiences, such as the Pokemon Go app, generated over $3 billion in global revenue in 2018. XR is also the user interface into the metaverse, the idea of a virtual universe where we can be whoever or whatever we want, while exploring the digital world of gaming, meeting up, going to events, or anything along the lines of the movie 'Ready Player One'.
But accessibility and availability are obvious obstacles to overcome, given that XR headsets can be pricey, bulky, and clunky. But the technology will become more common, affordable, and comfortable to use, which will only increase the chance of widespread use. The biggest challenges will include privacy and the potential mental and physical impacts of highly immersive technologies.
3D Printing
3D printing, also known as additive manufacturing, means creating a 3D object from a digital file by building it layer by layer. 3D printing may seem distinctly more low-tech than artificial intelligence or gene editing, but it has the potential to completely transform manufacturing and other industries.
Using 3D printing, the factories of the future could quickly print spare parts for machinery on site. Entire assembly lines could be replaced with 3D printers. We could print human tissue for transplant, print weapons, even print food.
3D printing technology brings many opportunities, but it also brings some downsides, challenges, and obstacles to overcome. While it has the potential to reduce the environmental impact of manufacturing by using fewer materials overall, we have to consider the environmental impact of the printers themselves.
3D printing also presents problems for intellectual property owners, since the technology enables counterfeiters to produce fake license goods cheaply and easily. There's also the problem that weapons can be easily 3D printed. One thing I find particularly exciting about 3D printing is the potential it brings for mass personalization of products. Thanks to 3D printing, products and Designs can be customized to suit one-off requests in orders, and this could cover anything from personalized sneakers to food that's personalized to our individual nutritional needs.
Keep an eye on these technologies, as I believe they have the biggest potential to impact the future of human life and our society. To stay on top of these and other trends, sign up for my newsletter, and check out my books ‘Tech Trends in Practice’ and ‘Business Trends in Practice.'

title: Council Post: The Road To Maturity: Why It’s Finally Time For AI In CX To Grow Up
text:
Chief Marketing Officer at Interactions, a conversational AI company, where he oversees all aspects of communications, sales and marketing.
Most of us are all too familiar with the pitfalls of automated customer service. It’s a predictable and painful cycle: call a business, meet a clunky automated system and repeat yourself in an effort to be understood — “billing … billing … BILLING.” Of course, that’s only until you hang up or get redirected to a busy agent queue and, already frustrated, wait on hold with a repeating message that states, “We value you as a customer.”
As the first point of interaction between businesses and their customers, customer service has always been ripe for disruption. Over the last decade, brands have invested heavily in automated solutions to offload repetitive tasks from agents and drive more efficient, seamless and personalized customer experiences (CX). And we’ve seen some progress — from dial menus to interactive voice response solutions (IVRs) and AI-powered voice assistants.
However, customer service today remains one of the most annoying automation applications when companies don’t implement it correctly. This is hard to believe given the potential value on the table; Salesforce research found that 63% of customers say they will pay more for a great experience. The problem, in my opinion, stems from a fallacy in the customer service world: that AI must only be used as a tool to support agents. Instead, I believe AI should lead the experience with the personalization and efficacy consumers seek while agents work in the background to maintain a vital human touch. In the spirit of reflection and improvement that comes during the new year, I’m taking a look at how AI in the customer experience has matured over time and why I believe it’s finally time for AI to truly grow up.
The Growth Spurt That Wasn’t
In the infancy of the AI boom, brands touted a completely new customer experience — one that eliminated wait times, allowed consumers to manage inquiries without agent support and incorporated a 360-degree view of the customer. Over the years, we’ve seen funding pour into this industry and an extraordinary number of new startups emerge — but even so, the capabilities often don’t live up to the hype. IVRs are the perfect example of this. Everyone has encountered a menu that prompts them to “press one to make a payment” or offers a list of select words they can use to convey their purpose. Businesses control the conversation with specific word recognition that ultimately turns customers over to agents. While IVRs were expected to streamline interactions and support customer demand, recent research from eGain (via Yahoo!) suggests that they’ve done little to deliver on the hype.
The Teen Years of Human-Technology Collaboration
In the teen years, we all (including AI) start to come into our own — but not without some growing pains. As AI became more sophisticated and picked up momentum, many companies turned to solutions that automated for efficiency but offered more natural dialogue. Advances in natural language processing have accelerated this trend, powered a better understanding of customer speech and fostered more human-like interactions. But to get there, I’ve found that businesses have had to come to an important realization: Humans would always be needed to unlock the technology’s full potential, whether that’s through eliminating bias or managing sudden change.
With this realization came a fundamental shift in the agent experience. New companies emerged with the specific goal of helping agents manage inquiries. Some offer prompts for what to say next, while others analyze emotions to provide insights into customer sentiment. So far, businesses have largely relied on agents to lead customer service and leveraged AI to help them do their jobs.
AI, All Grown Up
Enter the pandemic — a moment of reckoning for the customer service industry amid disrupted business practices, shifting consumer behaviors and high demand.
After taking stock of how the industry has evolved, it’s clear to me that we’ve strained the existing systems as far as they can go — and, in doing so, have underscored the need for a new model. Rather than using AI as a support pillar for agents, I believe businesses should leverage it as the interface for customer service to provide customers with the efficacy, efficiency and personalization that they seek.
This is not to say that agents shouldn’t play a key role in customer service; we learned in the teen phase that we’ll always need the human touch. However, we can rethink their role. On a recent episode of my company’s podcast, I spoke with Frida Polli, co-founder and CEO of AI-powered talent-matching platform pymetrics. She shared that she believes it’s important for companies to audit their data and ensure that their AI isn’t trained with flawed data sets. If we extrapolate that learning to customer service, I believe we should use human expertise to help AI understand specific speech patterns, accents and phrasing in real time and enable it to adapt to customer needs and improve with each interaction.
Turning today’s CX paradigm on its head is no easy feat, but there are steps leaders can take to get a head start. First and foremost, assess what defines a successful interaction for your business, but do it from the perspective of the customer. Is it customer satisfaction scores (CSATs)? Is it lower customer effort scores (CES)? Or is there a broader benchmark that reflects ongoing engagement? Once you’ve determined what success looks like, engage with your agents to understand where they can be most impactful in tracking toward this goal and outline their new AI-supported role accordingly. If we allow AI to come into its own and collaborate with agents to excel in this new paradigm, we may finally realize the industry’s long-promised vision.
The new year is typically a time to reflect on growth and room for improvement in the future, so naturally, I’ve been doing that for my own industry. While AI applications have made tremendous strides since their infancy, they still need a little nudge to truly reach adulthood. A report from ReportLinker (via GlobeNewswire) expects the global contact center market size to reach $496 billion by 2027, so I think it’s time to explore ways for AI to drive the industry forward and finally put those “billing … BILLING” phone calls to rest.

title: Council Post: How An AI System Can Predict Critical Events And Help Reduce Their Impact
text:
Dustin Radtke is the CTO at OnSolve, a leading critical event management provider for enterprises, SMBs and government entities.
Over the last two years, we've experienced increasingly persistent and worsening critical events globally — catastrophic weather, civil unrest, the pandemic, cyberattacks. According to a Forrester study commissioned by my company, OnSolve, 99% of organizations experienced a critical event in the last 18 months, and over half believe their organizations are ineffective at responding across critical risk categories. Because they're underprepared, leaders often only react after a crisis occurs rather than preparing ahead of time. The results can be catastrophic.
Protecting stakeholders and assets is one of an organization's biggest responsibilities. To improve organizational resilience and ensure continuity, leaders need a plan to proactively identify, mitigate and respond to risks.
Dealing With Data In Real Time
One of the biggest hurdles to overcome is the sheer amount of data to process in a timely manner. Organizations can easily get overwhelmed by incoming signals and internal data surrounding their assets and people.
Nearly 30% of global data will be real-time by 2025, so organizations need a way to parse data quickly to find relevant threat insights. Even large organizations with risk analyst teams are buried in data, and smaller organizations without these resources are more easily swamped.
The lack of real-time data creates a reactive crisis response. This makes artificial intelligence (AI) an important part of critical event management. It helps enterprise, industry and government entities better understand and, at times, predict what kind of impact an evolving threat can have on their stakeholders and assets.
AI helps organizations prepare for critical events before they occur. If a tornado is approaching a warehouse, for example, AI can triangulate warning signals and share alerts with decision-makers with corresponding crisis response recommendations. By uncovering the threat in advance, organizations can shift operations to a different location to reduce the disruptions and keep employees safe. Early detection is only possible with real-time data.
If an event unfolds in real time without any advance warning, organizations can understand what's happening and respond quickly to reduce potential impact. For example, if there's a closure of a major highway used for logistics routes, AI can alert leadership much faster than traditional alerting systems (like word of mouth or reading about the news online). This buys management time to find new routes or alternative sourcing opportunities, re-route their teams and communicate to the right people of any changes to plans or delays.
How AI Produces Actionable Intelligence
Before insights get to leaders for action, there's a six-step process to turn raw data into actionable intelligence to ensure high quality alerts:
1. Ingest. Through machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) algorithms, AI systems ingest both structured data (like information from government bureaus or geological services/weather data) and unstructured data (like social media).
2. Clean. Raw data feeds will always include irrelevant data regardless of how reliable the sources are. It's critical for ML to clean the data and remove the noise so all that's left is valuable information.
3. Classify. There's a wide range of threats and threat categories from natural disasters to geopolitical, and AI classifies data to prepare it for further analysis.
4. Locate. Once cleaned and classified, ML and NLP find, disambiguate and resolve the event location in a process called geoparsing. Once the location is determined, it's correlated against an organization's people, property or assets to assess potential impact.
5. Detect. Once the "where" is determined, AI reviews the sources to determine the date and time of an event to extrapolate exactly when the critical event occurred.
6. Cluster. To cut down on needless noise, the system looks for similarities in event details to label and cluster alerts for the same event.
Once the AI engine has predicted that an event will occur or has occurred, it measures the impact that threat could have, then alerts leadership. This is a critical step — without AI, the knowledge of the event and its effects could take minutes, hours or days to reach leadership. By relying on traditional human processes to manage critical events, businesses operate in a reactive state instead of proactively mitigating the impact.
AI can also activate an organization's crisis playbook to guide response and management of a critical event, such as an active assailant or looting at a store, with automated workflows and critical communications. AI can also help improve future response by learning from past response plans and automate the pre-determined, manual activities. While AI cannot predict when severe weather will hit or when a riot will occur, it can provide real-time insight into those unplanned threats. This allows leaders to minimize the impact and inform accurate crisis management when time is of the essence.
How To Build An AI-Based System For Critical Event Management
When implementing an AI system for crisis management, consider the following:
• Build in the cloud. Cloud-based systems are more resilient, faster, more accessible and cost-effective since you don't need to maintain the environments. Even if you lose power at your server facility (a crisis in itself), you'll still have access to your systems.
• Use a single point of truth. When a crisis occurs, you don't want to waste time managing multiple systems. Instead, use one workflow that brings all the information together so leadership works from a unified playbook.
• Automate whenever possible. It's critical to be able to communicate with your stakeholders as quickly as possible. Automation increases response time and reduces human error.
• Build a system that can continuously grow and update. Organizations' needs change and new technology or data sources will be available. Create a system that's flexible enough to grow with your organization. Technically speaking, working with vendors or creating solutions that have "open APIs" creates room for your organization to build and integrate with other technology solutions you may need now or in the future.
Though critical events are increasing, with technology like AI, organizations have more solutions than ever to proactively predict, manage and respond to crises. By implementing ML and NLP, you can overcome traditional limitations to save lives and protect your organization when every minute counts.

title: Survey Of AI Teams Points To Promise And Peril Ahead
text:
The AI revolution is here. Machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence are used in virtually every industry today to revolutionize everything from reducing food waste to achieving better health outcomes. In all, IDC forecasts that global enterprise spending on AI will eclipse $204 billion by 2025.
Unfortunately, investments in needed infrastructure may not be keeping pace. Many enterprises are shipping AI blind or relying on outdated model monitoring approaches to catch issues with models in production.
In order to understand the scope of the problem and provide insights on potential solutions, Arize AI recently conducted a survey of 945 data scientists, engineers, executives, and others in the industry. The results speak to a distinct need for better tools to quickly visualize where and why problems are emerging and enable faster root cause analysis when models fail.
Here are three of the survey’s key findings – and recommendations about what enterprise executives and their ML teams can do about them.
The Need for Speed and Easier Troubleshooting
Survey says: Despite progress, today’s day-to-day reality for ML teams is frequently painful and slow.
84.3% of data scientists and ML engineers say the time it takes to detect and diagnose problems with a model is an issue for their teams at least some of the time – likely exacerbated by a post-pandemic environment where drift and performance issues are elevated. In all, over half of data scientists, ML engineers and technical executives say their teams would benefit from deeper capabilities around drift monitoring and troubleshooting; over four in ten want better model performance monitoring.
Recommendation: Evaluate and implement an ML observability platform that helps expose and eliminate AI blindspots.
Virtually all AI teams monitor known knowns – model metrics such as accuracy, AUC, F1, etc. Most also try to address black box AI — known unknowns — through explainability. However, often what’s still missing are solutions that expose the issues teams are not actively looking for: blindspots, or unknown unknowns. True ML observability can help eliminate blindspots by automatically surfacing hidden problems before they impact business results. Rather than writing seemingly interminable queries to get to the bottom of performance degradation, teams using a modern ML observability platform can quickly visualize the full array of potential problems and perform root cause analysis in a few clicks. Procurement guides on product and technical requirements to consider when assessing an ML monitoring and observability platform can help.
Closing Team Gaps
Survey says: A chasm exists between executives and AI teams.
Despite the fact that ML models are more critical to business results in the wake of COVID-19 for nearly one-third of those surveyed, 54.0% report issues with business executives not being able to quantify AI ROI somewhat often or somewhat often. Meanwhile, 19.3% of technical executives say that they often encounter issues around sharing data.
Recommendation: Grow internal visibility, increase AI literacy, and quantify AI ROI.
As AI becomes increasingly important to business-critical operations, the technical teams deploying ML models and their executive counterparts need to be in total alignment. Unfortunately, this is proving elusive according to the survey. The way out is straightforward: business executives need increased education, access to tools and digestible, relevant KPIs – including, most importantly, a way to quantify AI ROI. By tying model performance metrics to key business metrics and giving executives access to tools that visualize these metrics over time, ML teams can ensure broader buy-in for their efforts.
Explainability
Survey says: Explainability – the ability to understand how a model came to a particular decision – is important, but it isn’t everything.
Although technical executives and data scientists place high importance on explainability, certain industries and ML engineers – who are generally the ones getting models into production and maintaining them once there – place higher importance on monitoring and troubleshooting drift and data quality issues.
Recommendation: Do not rely on explainability alone; take a proactive approach to model performance management.
Focusing on explainability in the pre-production phases of the model lifecycle – training a model and validating it before deployment – can be useful. However, continuing to expend the bulk of resources on explainability once a model is in production is of limited utility since it creates a passive feedback loop. In other words, while explainability is useful for sorting when troubleshooting model performance in production, it does not help you surface blindspots the same way that data quality monitoring helps proactively catch potential issues before a substantial shift in inference distributions occurs, for example. By setting up automated performance monitors across a given model, ML teams can have a first line of defense — especially if able to A/B compare datasets and perform data quality checks. Drift monitoring across environments or prior periods of production can also be an early signal that model outputs are shifting.
Conclusion
While these are hardly the only issues facing the teams building AI systems, they are some of the most salient according to a broad cross-section of practitioners and executives surveyed. Hopefully quantifying some of the common problems among teams can help shine a spotlight on the way forward.

title: The Ethical Debate About Whether AI Ought To Warn You When The Self-Driving Car That You Are Riding In Is About To Crash
text:
We’ve all likely had our share of car crashes over the years.
Let’s trace the various published research underlying a somewhat simple but altogether crucial question, namely if you know that a crash is about to occur should you go limp or attempt to tighten and brace yourself. Turns out that the answer is complicated and often dependent upon the circumstances at hand.
First, there is a popular assumption that you ought to let your body go loose or limp when an impending car crash is about to occur. Some claim that this ragdoll posturing will be advantageous. The purported logic is that we all know that a straight and narrow stick will presumably break and snap entirely when placed under intense pressure. As such, if you tense up, you are risking all manner of personal bodily damage.
According to the sage wisdom of Confucius: “The reed which bends in the wind is stronger than the mighty oak which breaks in a storm.”
I don’t believe though that Confucius had an opportunity to drive or ride in an automobile (he lived from 551 BC to 479 BC, while cars were essentially invented in the late 1880s).
Some counterarguments clearly indicate you would be unwise to simply go into a sagging status. Without properly bracing yourself for an impact, you are presumably going to let your body and limbs be without any kind of protective limbering. The analogy is often used about football players. A football player that is braced for getting tackled and struck hard by another player is generally going to be much better off than a football player that is unaware of the smacking and has let down their muscular guard.
As such, the assertion is that you would be wiser to do some appropriate pre-bracing before an imminent car crash. The use of your existing muscles can potentially serve to reduce the injury severity that is going to be entailed. A passive response occupant is seemingly at the whim of whatever happens, and their body will be without any formal resistance and nor protective guidance. Various research studies have used musculoskeletal models to examine these types of differences.
Let’s once again lean into Confucius: “Success depends upon previous preparation, and without such preparation, there is sure to be a failure.”
In that sense, an argument can be made that you ought to prepare yourself appropriately when a car crash is about to occur. One way to prepare yourself is to brace your body and get ready for the multitude of forces that will impinge upon it.
Another concern about going lifeless is that if you are the driver of the vehicle, you are ostensibly giving up any further chance of directing the car. According to the extreme version of the just-let-go precept, the driver’s hands and arms would potentially fall to their side and no longer be on the wheel (because they have relaxed all their muscles that would otherwise keep their hands and arms in a commanding position). The driver would no longer be trying to use the brake or the accelerator to possibly avert the crash or lessen the impact of the crash.
Do we really want a driver to become like a lump of clay when sitting at the driving controls?
You might try to retort that the driver would only do this when they had determined that absolutely no other recourse was possible. In essence, the driver has ascertained that the car crash is going to occur. The driver has further figured out that there is nothing else that can be done as the driver. All hope is lost. The crash is inevitable and nothing about any driving actions can avoid it. Likewise, no drivable action can be taken to reduce the impacts thereupon.
To some, this seems like a dubious proposition. The chances of not being able to take any driving actions would seem somewhat remote. Sure, maybe with a millisecond left to go, all options are now exhausted. But would the human driver have been able to make this decision to relax and wait until that fatal split second to do so?
Also, suppose the crash occurs and the car goes careening in some drivable direction. At this juncture, perhaps the car can be commanded. Unfortunately, the human driver has placed themselves into a mummy-like state and the odds of immediately recovering to then take the wheel actively would seem slim. Instead, the argument goes, the driver should be remaining alert and active, the entire time, hopeful that after the crash occurs there will still be opportunities to assuage additional injury by steering or using the pedals.
And what about the passengers?
Well, obviously the passengers are not at the wheel of the car. Ergo, they cannot directly affect how the car is going to proceed. In that manner of conditions, the passenger can seemingly choose to go limp or remain resolute, since they are then only dealing with themselves and not with the commanding of the car.
There is another potential downside to the notion of bracing yourself. Some people do absolutely the wrong thing, at the worst of times. For example, a person might freak out and decide to extend their legs upward and onto the dashboard, rather than remaining in a fully seated position. This is almost always a bad idea. You are indubitably increasing the chance of breaking your legs.
The point being that getting yourself braced has to be done with a dose of sensibility. This comes up in those heated discussions about whether to go limp or get tense. The person arguing against going tense will bring up the foolish acts that some take when getting themselves braced. This is kind of unfair because it suggests that all that opt to prepare themselves will do so in that manner. A base assumption is that most people will simply remain in their seated position and tense their muscles, rather than trying to change their positions altogether.
This provides an open avenue of attack against the going limp proponents.
Here’s the rub.
A person that goes lifeless might find themselves no longer in the protective zone of the personal safety restraints of the vehicle. The odds are that the car has safety belts. The odds are too that the car has airbags. Your body and limbs need to be in the sweet spot for those safety features to succeed at their best potential. The concern then is that a limp person might not have their body in a posture that no longer gets maximal protection from the purposely provided safety restraints.
That’s a darned shame.
Imagine all the engineering and research into devising today’s modern safety restraints for cars. Tons of work has been done on this. In addition, it is costly for automakers to include these capabilities. All told, the intent is to make things safer for people inside cars. Yet, it is conceivable that people will subvert those safety restraints, at times by an overt wish to do so and in other cases by simply doing things that they didn’t think through and have left them adrift of that safety net.
Since we are discussing passengers, I have a rather vexing question for you.
Would you want to know if the car you are in is about to get into a severe car crash?
Oftentimes, a passenger is not paying attention to the roadway, since there is no particular need for them to do so. When a car crash is about to arise, the passenger might not have any clue that the dangerous situation is brewing. One minute, the passenger was happily looking at cat videos on their smartphone, and the next minute the lights went out. Boom. Bash. The passenger has been caught completely by surprise.
In some cases, a passenger might be watching the roadway and realize that a crash is imminent. Thus, they see this with their own eyes. Another possibility is that the passenger sees the driver doing something radically wild, and this is a likely sign that a crash is about to happen. Yet another means of gauging that crash might occur is by the motion of the car, such as the forces shoving you into your seat or swaying you over, due to drastic maneuvers taking place by the driver.
I’ll add one more means to realize that a crash is about to happen.
The driver tells you so.
When I say that the driver tells you, it might be more appropriate to say that the driver screams out that a crash is going to happen. Unless the driver has nerves of steel, it seems unlikely they would calmly look over at a passenger and in a monotone voice simply report that the vehicle is about to get into a horrific crash. This seems to be portrayed in movies, but in real life, the odds are pretty low that a driver would be so stoic.
The yelling approach might be applicable in that it would seem to get the attention of the passengers. A whispered or soft tone would be less likely to grab your focus. A bellowing outcry that a crash is going to occur would get the passengers alerted, one would so assume.
Why would the driver give such notification to the passengers?
Under the likely thinking that this will allow the passengers to ready themselves. That’s a nice thing to do. Without this kind of notification, the passenger is potentially unaware that some injurious smashing and maybe even rolling of the car is about to happen.
Some passengers would be thankful for any kind of heads-up before a car crash. Others might say they didn’t want to know. They would rather be caught by surprise. The act of knowing that a car crash is imminent would get their hearts pounding and strike fear in them. They would rather merely go with the punches and take their chances versus having to endure those moments beforehand of being cognizant that life for them is about to change and be in sheer terror.
Speaking of cars, the future of cars consists of AI-based true self-driving cars.
There isn’t a human driver involved in a true self-driving car. Keep in mind that true self-driving cars are driven via an AI driving system. There isn’t a need for a human driver at the wheel, and nor is there a provision for a human to drive the vehicle. For my extensive and ongoing coverage of Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) and especially self-driving cars, see the link here.
Here’s an intriguing question that is worth pondering: What should an AI-based true self-driving car do when it detects an imminent and unavoidable car crash in terms of alerting any passengers therein?
I’d like to first further clarify what is meant when I refer to true self-driving cars.
Understanding The Levels Of Self-Driving Cars
As a clarification, true self-driving cars are ones that the AI drives the car entirely on its own and there isn’t any human assistance during the driving task.
These driverless vehicles are considered Level 4 and Level 5 (see my explanation at this link here), while a car that requires a human driver to co-share the driving effort is usually considered at Level 2 or Level 3. The cars that co-share the driving task are described as being semi-autonomous, and typically contain a variety of automated add-on’s that are referred to as ADAS (Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems).
There is not yet a true self-driving car at Level 5, which we don’t yet even know if this will be possible to achieve, and nor how long it will take to get there.
Meanwhile, the Level 4 efforts are gradually trying to get some traction by undergoing very narrow and selective public roadway trials, though there is controversy over whether this testing should be allowed per se (we are all life-or-death guinea pigs in an experiment taking place on our highways and byways, some contend, see my coverage at this link here).
Since semi-autonomous cars require a human driver, the adoption of those types of cars won’t be markedly different than driving conventional vehicles, so there’s not much new per se to cover about them on this topic (though, as you’ll see in a moment, the points next made are generally applicable).
For semi-autonomous cars, it is important that the public needs to be forewarned about a disturbing aspect that’s been arising lately, namely that despite those human drivers that keep posting videos of themselves falling asleep at the wheel of a Level 2 or Level 3 car, we all need to avoid being misled into believing that the driver can take away their attention from the driving task while driving a semi-autonomous car.
You are the responsible party for the driving actions of the vehicle, regardless of how much automation might be tossed into a Level 2 or Level 3.
Self-Driving Cars And Car Crashes
For Level 4 and Level 5 true self-driving vehicles, there won’t be a human driver involved in the driving task.
All occupants will be passengers.
The AI is doing the driving.
One aspect to immediately discuss entails the fact that the AI involved in today’s AI driving systems is not sentient. In other words, the AI is altogether a collective of computer-based programming and algorithms, and most assuredly not able to reason in the same manner that humans can.
Why is this added emphasis about the AI not being sentient?
Because I want to underscore that when discussing the role of the AI driving system, I am not ascribing human qualities to the AI. Please be aware that there is an ongoing and dangerous tendency these days to anthropomorphize AI. In essence, people are assigning human-like sentience to today’s AI, despite the undeniable and inarguable fact that no such AI exists as yet.
With that clarification, you can envision that the AI driving system won’t natively somehow “know” about the facets of driving. Driving and all that it entails will need to be programmed as part of the hardware and software of the self-driving car.
Let’s dive into the myriad of aspects that come to play on this topic.
First, some pundits would refute the entire premise about the possibility of self-driving cars getting into any car crashes. These vocal provocateurs would claim that self-driving cars will be uncrashable. Because self-driving cars are apparently going to be uncrashable, there won’t be any need to ever warn a passenger about an imminent car crash. Case closed.
That’s pure nonsense.
Self-driving cars are going to get into car crashes.
As they say these days, period, full stop, drop the mic.
I’ve debunked the myth of self-driving cars being uncrashable, see the analysis at this link here.
In short, suppose a self-driving car is driving along, and a human driver that’s in a car behind the driverless car slams into the rear of the autonomous vehicle. Perhaps the human driver wasn’t paying attention and the self-driving car was slowing down or braking. Bam, the human driver plows into the self-driving car.
I realize that some will immediately exhort that this wasn’t the fault of the self-driving car (though we don’t know for sure that’s the case, since it could have been an improper braking action by the AI driving system). But putting aside the question of fault, the point is that the self-driving car did get entrenched in a car crash. No matter how good the AI driving system is at the driving task, there are still numerous exigencies that will come to play and car crashes are going to happen.
You can ostensibly shift this argument in a more sensible direction by contending that the number of car crashes will likely reduce due to the widespread adoption of self-driving cars. That stands to reason. In the United States alone there are about 6.7 million car crashes annually, encompassing about 2.5 million injuries and 40,000 fatalities (see my collection of stats at this link here). Many of those car crashes and the resulting sad and at times dire consequences can be attributed to human driving foibles. Humans drive while drunk, they drive while drowsy, they drive while distracted, etc. AI driving systems are presumably not going to make those kinds of human driving mistakes.
All told, those that are harping on the notion of zero fatalities due to self-driving cars are barking up the wrong tree. They are setting an utterly false expectation. This will serve to undermine the advent of self-driving cars by confusing the public when indeed self-driving cars get into car crashes. My seemingly harsh but apt comment is that zero fatalities have a zero chance of happening and we need to be more realistic about the adoption of self-driving cars.
Okay, I trust that you agree with me that there are going to be car crashes involving self-driving cars.
In that case, we can fruitfully turn to the question at hand. The gist is what if anything should the AI driving system do if it calculates or computes that a car crash is about to occur.
Keep in mind that we don’t know for sure that an AI driving system will necessarily have detected an impending car crash. It has a high potential for doing so, but this is not a guaranteed matter. The sensors used on self-driving cars consist of video cameras, radar, LIDAR, ultrasonic units, and the like. Whether or not the sensors can discern the nuances of a driving scene is not fully assured.
Furthermore, the AI driving system has to be sufficiently programmed to be able to try and identify that a car crash is potentially going to occur. This involves all kinds of probabilities and predictions. There is a fine line between absolutely being certain that a car crash is going to happen versus having some general probability that it might take place.
Another factor to keep in mind is how much time there is between the instant that a car crash prediction has taken place and the actual occurrence of the car crash. If the prediction happens with almost no time left before the crash itself, there is little time to do anything about the impending collision.
Let’s assume a scenario in which the AI driving system does calculate that a car crash is highly likely and that there is some substantive amount of time available to take various proactive actions.
What do we want the AI driving system to do?
One obvious factor would be to do whatever might be feasible to avoid the crash entirely. If that is not possible, then another approach would be to try and find ways to minimize the impacts of the car crash.
This is where I bring into play the famous or shall we say infamous Trolley Problem, see my explanation about this matter at this link here. The essence is that sometimes a self-driving car might need to make “ethical decisions” about what to do. For example, if the AI driving system could slightly turn the car so that it hits another car with less impact to the passengers inside the self-driving car, should the AI do this? Your answer would abundantly be yes.
But suppose the turning of the self-driving car is going to make the impact on the other car much harsher, likely harming more so the people inside that car. Now, a choice has to be made. Which is the right choice? That’s a tough ethical dilemma. Many people inside and outside of the self-driving car industry are right now eschewing these types of matters and pretending that they don’t exist. They do exist and they do matter.
Regrettably, few are exploring what to do.
Moving on, what else could the AI driving system do?
Some cars of all kinds are gradually being outfitted with external airbags. When a car equipped with external airbags is about to strike something hard, the airbags are deployed. This is similar to how airbags within the car are intended to protect the passengers. In the case of a self-driving car, we can anticipate that if the use of external airbags becomes prevalent, self-driving cars would likely have them too. As such, the AI driving system might deploy external airbags when a car crash seems likely.
We’ve now covered the aspect that involves actions that are pretty much outside of the self-driving car in terms of directing where the autonomous vehicle is going to go as part of the car crash and the use of external airbags as a safety measure.
Next, consider what might occur inside the self-driving car.
If there aren’t any passengers, this is one specific use case to consider. Recall that self-driving cars do not need to have any human inside at all. Conventional cars must have at least one human, the driver. For the instance of a self-driving car that has no occupants, there probably isn’t much to be done by the AI driving system about readying the interior of the vehicle.
We’ll shift into the use of having one or more passengers inside the self-driving car.
The AI driving system could potentially check to see if the passengers are properly seated. This could include whether they are wearing their seatbelts and figure out if they are in a proper position to take advantage of the internal airbags.
This brings us to the crux of the vexing question to be contemplated.
Should the AI driving system indicate to the passengers that a car crash is imminent?
As discussed earlier, some people might want to know and demand that they assuredly have to be told, while others might insist they don’t want to know. On the other hand, the odds are that this is a loosey-goosey kind of preference. A person that after the fact found out that they could have been notified and were not might have a change of heart and claim that had they been told they would have suffered less because of the car crash.
A darned if you do, darned if you don’t type of quandary.
The basis for suggesting to not warn the passengers is that they might freak out and make things worse for themselves. This takes us back to the matter of bracing oneself or opting to go limp as a ragdoll. You could somewhat argue that a warning by the AI driving system might end up causing more harm to the passengers rather than reducing the amount of harm.
Imagine too what the AI driving system would emit as a message.
Suppose it said that a car crash was about to occur.
Some passengers would find this a useless piece of information. It isn’t clear-cut what such a message portends. Is the AI driving system suggesting that the passenger should do something, or do nothing at all? This is completely lacking any sort of instructions.
In that manner, perhaps the AI driving system might emit a message that says that a car crash is about to occur and to ready yourself accordingly. I’m sure many would be puzzled and have no clue what “accordingly” means in that context.
Maybe the AI driving system would indicate that you should brace yourself for impact. The problem here is that we are all used to those customary “bracing” instructions on airlines about leaning forward and grabbing your ankles in a plane crash situation. That’s decidedly not going to be a wise move in most car crash scenarios.
Conclusion
There are plenty more twists and turns.
The odds are that self-driving cars will have new kinds of car seats that are somewhat unlike the seats in conventional human-driven cars. In a human-driven car, there has to be a seat at the driver’s position, thus allowing for access to the steering wheel and the driving controls. For a self-driving car, there aren’t any provided internal driving controls and the whole interior can be fully redesigned.
Some self-driving cars will likely have swivel seats. This allows you to look in whatever direction that you might wish to do so during a driving journey. The seats might also fully recline, allowing you to take a snooze or nap while the AI driving system is taking care of the driving for you.
In those various non-conventional positions of swiveling or laying down, will you be as protected during a car crash as when you were seated upright in a conventional car? If not, then presumably there might be something that the AI driving system could do to help out when a crash is about to occur.
The AI driving system could automatically force the swivel seats to go in a particular direction, such as facing forward (if that made the most sense from a crash injury-reducing perspective). For any seats in reclining mode, the AI driving system could force those seats to automatically prop up.
Here’s an intriguing thought for you.
Should the AI driving system do this without necessarily telling the passengers?
I ask because suppose that telling the passengers would be ineffective since the amount of time for humans to react would be insufficient to do anything. Meanwhile, the computer is operating at fast speeds that allow it to send electronic signals to the seats to swivel around or to prop up. In that case, the AI driving system might do so without necessarily alerting the passengers.
Of course, your reaction to having your seat suddenly swivel or prop up, as though with a mind of its own would be quite surprising and disconcerting. The reply to that qualm is that since this is only happening when a crash is going to occur, the passengers would not presumably have any time to be disquieted by the actions and would merely find themselves more safely positioned upon impact.
Back and forth this goes.
There’s a bit of a macabre joke amongst AI self-driving car insiders about these types of machinations.
If AI ever becomes sentient, might it decide that the “best” approach is to save the AI system that’s onboard the self-driving car, and ergo consider the human passengers as nothing more than added baggage? Thus, when choosing what to do, the AI will lean toward preserving the vehicle and the processors, more so than those pesky and irritating humans.
I guess we’ll need to deal with that someday, but for now, we can put that off today and cope with it tomorrow.
Perhaps that’s the kind of exhortation that Confucius might have proffered.

title: Machines are getting better at writing their own code. But human-level is 'light years away'
text:
Computers are getting better at writing their own code but software engineers may not need to worry about losing their jobs just yet.
DeepMind, a U.K. artificial intelligence lab acquired by Google in 2014, announced Wednesday that it has created a piece of software called AlphaCode that can code just as well as an average human programmer.
The London-headquartered firm tested AlphaCode's abilities in a coding competition on Codeforces — a platform that allows human coders to compete against one another.
"AlphaCode placed at about the level of the median competitor, marking the first time an AI code generation system has reached a competitive level of performance in programming competitions," the DeepMind team behind the tool said in a blogpost.
But computer scientist Dzmitry Bahdanau wrote on Twitter that human-level coding is "still light years away."
"The [AlphaCode] system ranks behind 54.3% participants," he said, adding that many of the participants are high school or college students who are just honing their problem-solving skills.
Bahdanau said most people reading his tweet could "easily train to outperform AlphaCode."
Researchers have been trying to teach computers to write code for decades but the concept has yet to go mainstream, partly because the AI tools that are meant to write new code have not been versatile enough.
An AI research scientist, who preferred to remain anonymous as they were not authorized to talk publicly on the subject, told CNBC that AlphaCode is an impressive technical achievement, but a careful analysis is required of the sort of coding tasks it does well on, versus the ones it doesn't.
The scientist said they believe AI coding tools like AlphaCode will likely change the nature of software engineering roles somewhat as they mature, but the complexity of human roles means machines won't be able to do the jobs in their entirety for some time.
"You should think of it as something that could be an assistant to a programmer in the way that a calculator might once have helped an accountant," Gary Marcus, an AI professor at New York University, told CNBC.
"It's not one-stop shopping that would replace an actual human programmer. We are decades away from that."
DeepMind is far from the only tech company developing AI tools that can write their own code.
Last June, Microsoft announced an AI system that can recommend code for software developers to use as they work.
The system, called GitHub Copilot, draws on source code uploaded to code-sharing service GitHub, which Microsoft acquired in 2018, as well as other websites.
Microsoft and GitHub developed it with help from OpenAI, an AI research start-up that Microsoft backed in 2019. The GitHub Copilot relies on a large volume of code in many programming languages and vast Azure cloud computing power.
Nat Friedman, CEO of GitHub, describes GitHub Copilot as a virtual version of what software creators call a pair programmer — that's when two developers work side-by-side collaboratively on the same project. The tool looks at existing code and comments in the current file, and it offers up one or more lines to add. As programmers accept or reject suggestions, the model learns and becomes more sophisticated over time.
The software makes coding faster, Friedman told CNBC. Hundreds of developers at GitHub have been using the Copilot feature all day while coding, and the majority of them are accepting suggestions and not turning the feature off, Friedman said.
In a separate research paper published on Friday, DeepMind said it had tested its software against OpenAI's technology and it had performed similarly.
Samim Winiger, an AI researcher in Berlin, told CNBC that every good computer programmer knows that it is essentially impossible to create "perfect code."
"All programs are flawed and will eventually fail in unforeseeable ways, due to hacks, bugs or complexity," he said.
"Hence, computer programming in most critical contexts is fundamentally about building 'fail safe' systems that are 'accountable.'"
In 1979, IBM said "computers can never be held accountable" and "therefore a computer must never make a management decision."
Winiger said the question of the accountability of code has been largely ignored despite the hype around AI coders outperforming humans.
"Do we really want hyper-complex, intransparent, non-introspectable, autonomous systems that are essentially incomprehensible to most and uncountable to all to run our critical infrastructure?" he asked, pointing to the finance system, food supply chain, nuclear power plants, weapons systems and space ships.
— Additional reporting by CNBC's Jordan Novet.

title: Council Post: Personalization And Context: AI’s Surging Role In Advertising
text:
Emilia Kirk is the Global Head of Growth at Seedtag, responsible for Client, Marketing and Product Growth. Visit Seedtag’s site to hear more
For years, brands have been using data to analyze their target audience’s online identity and behavior in order to strategize their advertising efforts. Now, as digital security continues to tighten and consumers become increasingly aware of the information companies can access, behavioral targeting is coming to a slow death. With this in mind, brands need to reevaluate their efforts to generate a sense of trust from their audiences, while delivering relevant ads.
Since the passing of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), consumer scrutiny over third-party data has grown. In conjunction, the sophistication of artificial intelligence (AI) expanded.
Defined by IBM as leveraging “computers and machines to mimic the problem-solving and decision-making capabilities of the human mind,” conceptually, AI has existed since the 1950s. For a while, it seemed to only appear as a fully formed technology in cinema.
However, over the course of the last decade, it is realizing its true potential. The world might not be at the level of entering the Matrix or being visited by future cyborg versions of Arnold Schwarzenegger, but driverless cars are no longer beyond the realms of possibility, and many now have spoken conversations with devices in their homes.
AI has come a long way. The technology is constantly learning and evolving, and on a broader business scale, it continues to be a cost-effective solution that automates tasks and enables greater, more informed decision-making.
Applying AI To The Advertising Industry
The brilliance of AI is in its application. As a technology, it is supremely agile and can be applied across almost any industry, with a deep catalogue of use cases within each. Yet, it has not yet reached its full potential within the advertising space. That is, up until now.
With behavioral targeting currently going through its swansong, an opportunity has now appeared for AI to swoop in and help brands collect, analyze and action data for their targeted ad campaigns.
The issue for many is the data itself. To mimic the problem-solving and decision-making capabilities of the human mind, it must first feed on the data required to make those decisions. Behavioral targeting is limited to utilizing third-party data, and incoming regulations essentially render that tactic redundant. However, the sophistication of AI can introduce a much wider pool of information that can be leveraged when it comes to targeting within campaigns.
Finding The Right Data
What data is still fair game? Rather than concentrating directly on consumer information themselves, it’s important to recognize the context behind their online behavior and purchasing decisions. Instead of following cookies across the internet, brands should turn their focus on publishing pages themselves, and the content that is being consumed.
High-quality publishers — which attract significant audience numbers on a regular basis — offer a wealth of data that can be utilized while remaining completely GDPR-compliant and non-reliant on private information.
AI’s capabilities allow brands to consider the context behind digital content. This includes not only keywords but page types, phrases and different media channels — and a wide range of other data that enables accurate targeting to individuals through their real-time interest.
This allows publishers to serve ads that fit better with the content of the page and also better cater to the tastes of the reader, providing them with a much more personalised and pleasant experience. Publishers can also make use of first-party data, which is the data users willingly give when signing up for newsletters, subscriptions, etc. This data, when combined with the contextual data tools that many publishers already use, allows publishers to better control and boost their ads revenues.
If a luxury vehicle manufacturer wanted to reach luxury consumers within the automotive industry, it would need to understand their interests first. Without the ability to peer into their cookie history, AI could instead be used to analyze trending topics and reach users segmented by specific contextual territories such as luxury, sustainability, fashion or sports, while observing competitors' territories to differentiate from and set apart. An extremely top-level example, but AI analyzes the context — down to the very last word to target consumers.
Target Acquired — What’s Next?
AI can create contextual targeting that helps brands reach the right audience, and while highly targeted ads lend themselves to being viewed as more attractive, enjoyable and interesting by users, brands can take their approach one step further to ensure a high-quality user experience.
Too often, consumers are greeted by digital ads that significantly disrupt their experience. Whether they’re pop-ups, interstitials or bland banner ads, the quality of ads that are typically served online can be poorly received. It comes as no surprise that the majority of online users from Generation Z right through to Baby Boomers find digital ads more annoying than memorable, according to research undertaken by Deloitte.
Through the use of AI, brands can also better understand the optimal ad placement on a page. With an almost human-like analysis of content — across text, image or video — AI can detect where to best place an ad, finding the sweet spot that ensures the ad is received in the best way possible. Combined with further effects that blend ads into images, videos or displays, advertisers can integrate their messages into visual content with ease, delivering impactful campaigns that provide a great return on investment.
Preparing For The Future
AI reads between the lines that humans can’t. With a deep level understanding of a myriad of data involved in the targeting process, not only would a manual replication of contextual targeting take hours — if not days — of work, but it would also be cluttered in errors, and the campaign would ultimately be ineffective.
Of course, AI isn't perfect. Concerns surrounding it need to be addressed in order for AI to be more widely adopted by publishers and brands — these include concerns over cybersecurity and individual privacy. This is especially important as consumers are used to privacy issues with pre-GDPR standards that allowed for more third-party data collection.
Regulations such as GDPR in Europe and the California Consumer Privacy Act, as well as Google’s plan to eliminate third-party cookies from Chrome, should go some way to alleviating those privacy concerns.
The advertising industry is still a long way from perfecting AI, but the technology has already proven itself to be hugely beneficial across a wide range of industries. From here, AI is poised to continually improve.
